smell: BuildSteps panics on ReRunSafeUnset but never propagates the value to builtStep, and Orchestrator.Run never queries it. ReRunSafeNo is decorative metadata — a step is still re-executed on a fresh run unless the StepDef ALSO supplies AlreadyDone. Out of 5 ReRunSafeNo steps in the codebase, only one (postinstall.StepCleanupBootstrap) provides a precondition guard.
severity_reason: rubric §4/un-idiomatic-pattern-bitten-repo: contract is half-wired and silently misleading. Operators reading setup.StepBuildISOs (ReRunSafeNo) assume orchestrator refuses re-run after partial completion, but it reruns unconditionally. Roadmap state:4f69fc9d itself documents this gap.
fix_summary: Either (a) make ReRunSafeNo + missing AlreadyDone fail BuildSteps so authors must wire a precondition, or (b) require a logger.Warn at orchestrator entry for ReRunSafeNo steps without AlreadyDone. Option (a) gives the contract teeth — every ReRunSafeNo step gets an AlreadyDone or the build panics. Cross-reference roadmap state:4f69fc9d (deferred).
rule_source: repo-counter-example: internal/distribution/okd/postinstall/steps.go:53-56 (StepCleanupBootstrap is the ONLY ReRunSafeNo step with a SkipWhen guard)
must_preserve: Canonical StepDef shape; BuildSteps panic-on-zero-value behaviour

smell: StepBuildISOs and StepUploadISOs are ReRunSafeNo but neither declares AlreadyDone. A SIGKILL mid-ISO-build leaves a partial fedora-coreos-master0.iso in workDir; mid-upload leaves a partial ISO on the Proxmox host. The next deploy re-runs the orchestrator from step 1; cleanup.WorkOnly removes custom-isos/ locally, but the partial remote upload is never sha256-verified before being referenced by the cdrom block in the bootstrap/master/worker resources.
severity_reason: rubric §4/data-loss-risk: a corrupted ISO booting a control-plane node yields a node that won't join the cluster and may need to be rebuilt by hand. Recovery path is undocumented.
fix_summary: Add AlreadyDone to StepBuildISOs that verifies SHA256 of every expected output ISO matches the cached fedora-coreos image hash; on mismatch, treat as 'work not done' and re-build. For StepUploadISOs, add AlreadyDone that runs `pvesh get /nodes/<node>/storage/<storage>/content` filtered to iso/<expected-name>.iso and verifies the size matches the local ISO. Either pre-condition stops a half-uploaded artifact from being treated as ready.

smell: writeDnsmasqConfig backs up the existing /etc/dnsmasq.d/<name>.conf via system.CopyFile (NOT atomic), then writes content to a temp file via system.WriteTempFile, then installs it via another system.CopyFile. CopyFile does Open+io.Copy+Sync+Close — NOT rename + fsync_dir. A SIGKILL between os.OpenFile(dst, O_TRUNC) and io.Copy completion leaves the live config truncated or partial. The validateAndRestartDnsmasq rollback hook fires only on validation/restart failure of the new config, not on process death. Next dnsmasq restart fails to parse and cluster DNS resolution breaks.
severity_reason: rubric §4/data-loss-risk: cluster DNS is load-bearing; a half-written drop-in stops dnsmasq, which stops api.<cluster>.<domain> resolution, which fails kubectl/oc and any operator manual recovery. Backup-and-CopyFile is a known-broken atomicity pattern.
fix_summary: Replace the WriteTempFile + CopyFile sequence with a single system.AtomicWriteString(configPath, content, 0o644) call. AtomicWrite already does temp-file + fsync + rename + parent-fsync on the same filesystem. Keep the existing .backup snapshot for the validateAndRestartDnsmasq rollback path. Net diff: -10 LOC.
must_preserve: validateAndRestartDnsmasq backup-restore flow on validation/restart failure

smell: installHAProxyConfig calls system.CopyFile(tmpPath, /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg) — NOT atomic. A SIGKILL between truncate and io.Copy completion leaves the live haproxy.cfg empty or partial; next `systemctl restart haproxy` fails to parse and the bastion stops fronting kube-api. The rollback path also uses CopyFileMode (also non-atomic), so a crash during rollback leaves the config in a third bad state.
severity_reason: rubric §4/data-loss-risk: haproxy is the sole api.<cluster> frontend during bootstrap and the *.apps frontend before update-ingress. A corrupted config breaks the bastion's role and the recovery path requires manual editing.
fix_summary: Replace the two CopyFile sites in haproxy.go (line 68 install, line 122 rollback restore) with system.AtomicWriteString(haproxyConfigPath, content, 0o644) reading the source file's content into memory first. Or factor a system.AtomicCopyFile that takes (src, dst, mode) and pipes the read into AtomicWrite. The backup snapshot at line 111 is not on the trust-boundary path so the existing CopyFile there is acceptable.
must_preserve: haproxy validation + rollback flow; backup snapshot before install

smell: --skip-terraform / --skip-cleanup / --skip-firewall are documented as 'no-op with --dry-run' but the dry-run path silently ignores them. destroyDryRun branches at line 100 and never inspects the skip flags. An operator running `okdctl destroy --dry-run --skip-terraform` reasonably expects a preview of what cleanup would do without terraform; instead they get only the terraform plan and zero hint that --skip-terraform was thrown away.
severity_reason: Footgun for scripted destroy — silent flag-drop violates principle of least surprise. Not a data-loss path because dry-run is read-only.
fix_summary: Either (a) make destroyDryRun honor the skip-* flags and emit a preview of what cleanup-files / cleanup-firewall WOULD do (e.g. list dnsmasq drop-in path, haproxy backup glob, firewall ports); or (b) at the entry point of runDestroy, when destroyDryRun is true and any skip-* flag is set, return a *errtypes.ConfigError so the operator sees 'flag X is incompatible with --dry-run' instead of silent acceptance. (b) is the safer default; (a) is the more useful UX but takes more LOC.
rule_source: repo-counter-example: internal/cli/cleanup.go:64-71 (cleanupDryRun is itself a side-effect-free print)

smell: runDestroyDryRun executes terraform init + terraform plan -destroy without acquiring the project runlock. A concurrent `okdctl deploy` running tf init in the same workDir can race the dry-run's tf init — both processes write to .terraform/, .terraform.lock.hcl, and providers/. Tf init has no internal mutex. Same hazard applies to runDeployDryRun (deploy.go:137). The runlock is the canonical concurrent-run guard (state:4c092fce, PR #118 landed it specifically for this).
severity_reason: rubric §4/un-idiomatic-pattern-bitten-repo: roadmap state:4c092fce (PR #118) explicitly added runlock to deploy + destroy + cleanup + update-ingress to prevent concurrent-tf-init corruption — dry-run paths were missed. A racing dry-run + live deploy can corrupt .terraform/ provider lock metadata.
fix_summary: Take a shared/non-blocking runlock in both runDestroyDryRun (destroy.go:175) and runDeployDryRun (deploy.go:137). On conflict, refuse with a clear message naming the holding verb. If dry-run + concurrent dry-run is desired, expose a runlock.AcquireShared helper using LOCK_SH instead of LOCK_EX — flock supports shared locks natively.
rule_source: roadmap.md §E1 state:4c092fce — concurrent-run lock with stale-PID detection (PR #118)

smell: terraformFilesToRemove still includes 'terraform.tfstate.backup'. Roadmap state:4c092fce:tf-state-backup-removed-on-success (marked done) split Cleanup → CleanupPlans in terraform.go to STOP wiping .backup, but cleanup/infra.go's Terraform cleanup hook still removes the backup directly. After destroy → orchestrator runs StepCleanupFiles → cleanup.Terraform → wipes terraform.tfstate.backup. The .backup file is the operator's last-resort rollback artefact when the live tfstate is later corrupted; sweeping it on every destroy makes stale-state recovery impossible.
evidence:
var terraformFilesToRemove = []string{
    "terraform.tfvars",
    "tfplan",
    "destroy.tfplan",
    "terraform.tfstate.backup",
    ".terraform.lock.hcl",
}
severity_reason: rubric §4/un-idiomatic-pattern-bitten-repo: same regression that roadmap state:4c092fce flagged in terraform.go (which fixed only HALF the problem). cleanup/infra.go does the same thing on a different path — partial fix.
fix_summary: Remove 'terraform.tfstate.backup' from terraformFilesToRemove. The .backup file is single-step rollback metadata; let the operator decide when to delete it (or add an explicit `okdctl cleanup --terraform-backup` flag). Net diff: -1 LOC.
rule_source: roadmap.md §state:4c092fce:tf-state-backup-removed-on-success — fixed in terraform.go but missed in cleanup/infra.go

smell: StepDestroyInfra is NonFatal=true so when terraform destroy fails midway the orchestrator continues to StepCleanupFiles → cleanup.Terraform → wipes terraform.tfvars + .terraform.lock.hcl + .terraform/. The next destroy retry has neither tfvars nor an init'd backend; tfvars encoded vmid_base + master_names + worker_names matching what is still alive on Proxmox, so re-running destroy fails with 'terraform.tfvars not found' and recovery is by hand.
severity_reason: rubric §4/data-loss-risk: not VM data loss, but operator-data loss — a partial-failed destroy is the worst time to wipe the configuration that recovers it. Re-run guidance does not exist; --skip-terraform is documented but assumes the operator knows the state is half-destroyed.
fix_summary: Make StepCleanupFiles consult the destroy tracker: if t.failures contains 'terraform destroy', set cleanupKind to a NEW 'TerraformPreserve' kind that skips Terraform() so the operator's tfvars stays. After a clean tf destroy success, run the full cleanup. Optionally also emit a clear log line: 'destroy: terraform failed, preserving tfvars / .terraform/ for retry — re-run okdctl destroy --skip-terraform=false to retry'.
must_preserve: existing skip-terraform flag semantics; destroy tracker labels

smell: tf.HasState() returns true for any non-empty terraform.tfstate file — but it's only checking system.FileExists, which doesn't distinguish a fresh empty `{}` state file from a populated one. After a tf init crashes mid-state-write, the file may exist with garbage or partial JSON. Destroy then runs `terraform plan -destroy` against a corrupt state and either fails confusingly or claims 'no changes' — the operator does not learn the state is corrupt.
severity_reason: State-corruption case is rare (terraform writes state atomically through its own backend), but okdctl can't detect it because HasState is a stat-check.
fix_summary: Either (a) parse the file as JSON and verify .resources is an array, or (b) shell out to `terraform state list` and check exit + non-empty output. (b) is safer because it handles all backend types (local, remote, http) without okdctl having to know the file shape.
rule_source: Go proverb: don't pretend to do work you can't
must_preserve: the no-state short-circuit so destroy is idempotent on a fresh project

smell: destroy is all-or-nothing at the cluster level. The CLI accepts --target=module.okd_cluster.proxmox_virtual_environment_vm.{bootstrap|master|worker}[N] (validated against the destroyTargetRE allowlist) but offers NO higher-level scoping like 'destroy only workers' or 'destroy only the bootstrap'. An operator who wants to bring up a fresh worker pool without disturbing masters must hand-craft N --target args matching destroyTargetRE.
severity_reason: Friction in a recovery-adjacent flow — a partial recovery often means 'rebuild workers but keep control plane'. Documented in audit rule catalog as `destroy-all-or-nothing`.
fix_summary: Add a --only={vms,workers,masters,bootstrap} flag that expands into the destroyTargetRE-matching --target list. Existing --target stays for power users; --only is the ergonomic alias.

smell: The package doc admits the design honestly: 'Cleanup is best-effort: a mid-run crash leaves workDir in a partially-removed state with no resume capability.' A two-pass design with .cleanup-plan.json was sketched but never implemented. The Full Kind runs WorkDirectory → WebServer → HAProxy → Apache → Dnsmasq → Terraform → Packages serially; a SIGKILL after WebServer leaves haproxy/apache/dnsmasq running with stale config, terraform.tfvars present, and no resume signal in the workDir.
severity_reason: Author-acknowledged debt; the existing serial flow is functional but not resumable. Not a blocker because the destroy/cleanup ordering is already 'safest-first'. Roadmap state:4f69fc9d covers the broader resume-checkpoint gap.
fix_summary: Lift cleanup.Execute's switch onto distribution.StepDef + BuildSteps so each subsystem cleanup becomes a step with AlreadyDone hooks. Subsystem-specific 'is removed' check: dnsmasq → !system.FileExists(/etc/dnsmasq.d/okd-<name>.conf), haproxy → !system.FileExists(haproxy backup) AND !system.IsServiceActive(haproxy), terraform → !system.FileExists(terraform.tfvars). A re-run becomes naturally resumable. Cross-references roadmap state:4f69fc9d.
must_preserve: removal ordering (work → web → services → terraform → packages); critical-path guard in refuseCriticalPath

smell: CleanupBootstrap re-init's terraform and runs `tf plan -target=module.okd_cluster.proxmox_virtual_environment_vm.bootstrap -var bootstrap_enabled=false`. The SkipWhen guard at postinstall/steps.go:53-56 only checks tfvars existence — but if tfvars exists with bootstrap_enabled already false (e.g. operator re-ran update-ingress after a prior successful bootstrap cleanup), the plan is a no-op and the apply silently succeeds. There's no AlreadyDone that asks 'is the bootstrap VM still alive?' before planning.
severity_reason: Wasted work — extra terraform init + plan + apply round-trip per re-run, but no correctness damage. ReRunSafeNo is overcautious here because tf -target apply is naturally idempotent.
fix_summary: Add AlreadyDone that probes Proxmox for the bootstrap VM's existence (via a pvesh lookup). Or downgrade to ReRunSafeYes since terraform -target apply with a destroy diff is idempotent. The cheapest fix: change ReRunSafe to ReRunSafeYes (matches reality) and drop the SkipWhen tfvars-existence guard since tf init will fail loudly if tfvars are missing.
must_preserve: the targeted-destroy of bootstrap only; idempotent semantics

smell: retrieveProvisionResult derives every VM IP from cfg.Networking.StaticIP.Start by IP arithmetic — it never asks Proxmox or terraform output what the apply ACTUALLY produced. If a network ordering bug or a parallel-apply race causes terraform to assign a different IP (or fail to assign one), okdctl's downstream wait-for-bootstrap polls a phantom IP and times out at 30 minutes with no diagnostic that the IP scheme drifted. The mutation invariant ('all Proxmox mutations MUST flow through terraform.Executor') does NOT forbid reads from `terraform output -json`.
severity_reason: Assumes terraform's apply matches okdctl's deterministic IP arithmetic, which holds today but is fragile to terraform-provider-proxmox version bumps that change resource ordering.
fix_summary: Add a `tf output -json` call after Apply succeeds (Provider.Provision around terraform.go:175). Compare each derived IP against the terraform-reported address (when terraform exposes it via outputs.tf — which it currently does for control_plane_ips/worker_ips). Mismatch → log a Warn naming both values and prefer the terraform-reported one. Cheap, defense-in-depth, no architectural change.
must_preserve: the 'all mutations through terraform' invariant; do NOT add a Proxmox HTTP client

smell: No code path in okdctl reads `.terraform_version` from terraform.tfstate. If a checkout uses Terraform 1.10 (versions.tf >= 1.10, < 2.0) but the existing state was written by a future 1.x where the schema bumps, okdctl's destroy path runs tf init → tf plan -destroy and trusts terraform's compatibility behaviour. Terraform 1.x is mostly forward-compat but cross-major boundary is enforced only at terraform itself; okdctl should stat the state's recorded terraform_version and refuse on a mismatch with versions.tf bound, not silently let terraform issue an error after init succeeds.
evidence:
tfDir := filepath.Join(projectRoot, "infrastructure", "terraform", "environments", tfEnv)
// tf := terraform.New(tfDir, ...) — no version pre-check
fix_summary: Pre-flight: jq .terraform_version terraform.tfstate, parse semver, refuse if it crosses the major boundary declared in versions.tf. Optional — terraform itself issues a clear error.

smell: Master resource has no `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }`. The block comment at line 244-246 acknowledges Terraform requires a literal boolean for prevent_destroy and recommends an override.tf as workaround — but the default ships unprotected. A rogue --target=module.okd_cluster.proxmox_virtual_environment_vm.master[N] passes the destroyTargetRE allowlist and destroys an etcd-quorum member with zero terraform-side guard. Roadmap iac:18a795d5 (deferred) covers this exactly.
severity_reason: rubric §4/data-loss-risk: etcd quorum loss requires offline rebuild from cluster-backup; a typo'd --target on master[N] is single-keystroke catastrophic. Defense-in-depth at the HCL layer is the single highest-value guard.
fix_summary: Add `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` to the master resource literal-mode (drop the var dependency). For the legitimate okdctl destroy path, gate behind a separate module flavour or document the override.tf escape hatch in the destroy CLI's --help. Cross-reference roadmap iac:18a795d5:hcl-no-prevent-destroy-masters.
rule_source: Terraform best-practices: prevent_destroy on stateful resources

smell: executeFullDeployment catches errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) at three phase boundaries (Prepare, Install, Configure) and prints InterruptSummary + 'run okdctl destroy to clean up'. But the workdir at this point may have partial ISOs, partial ignition, partial terraform state. The user is told 'run destroy' but destroy then runs through cleanup which wipes terraform.tfvars (see state:15ba17da above), so the *first* destroy retry might fail. There's no 'partial-deploy-detected' diagnostic and no checkpoint file to drive a smarter cleanup decision.
severity_reason: Documentation/UX gap. The current message points at destroy which CAN recover but the operator has no guidance on which --skip-* flags to use if the next destroy partial-fails. Pure observability: the underlying cleanup is correct.
fix_summary: Persist a small .okdctl-deploy-state.json under workDir on each phase entry (just the phase name + run-id + timestamp) and read it back at destroy time. If the file says 'install phase' or 'postinstall phase', destroy emits 'partial deploy detected — terraform state likely populated, will run destroy first' versus 'cancel during setup — terraform state is empty, run okdctl cleanup instead'. Cross-references roadmap state:4f69fc9d resume-checkpoint.

smell: StepCleanupBootstrap and StepDeployProductionDNS are NonFatal=true and mutate cluster-external state. If StepCleanupBootstrap succeeds (bootstrap VM gone) but StepVerifyKubeVIP fails, StepDeployProductionDNS skips on KubeVIPVerified=false. Result: bootstrap destroyed, DNS still pointing at bastion. Re-running deploy misses the bootstrap; re-running update-ingress can't reconcile production DNS because there is no resume-from-postinstall verb. Roadmap state:fb54208a (deferred) covers this.
severity_reason: Operator-recovery friction; the cluster keeps working with bastion-pointed DNS. Roadmap fb54208a tracks this; deferred severity matches.
fix_summary: Per roadmap fb54208a fix (b): expand `okdctl update-ingress` to handle the bootstrap→production DNS transition when DNS is still bootstrap-pointed (dns.IsBootstrapDNS already exists at update_ingress.go:70). Today update-ingress reconciles bootstrap-DNS → production-DNS only when LBs are detected; teach it to also handle the kube-vip-only path.
must_preserve: NonFatal semantics on bootstrap cleanup + DNS; ReRunSafe declarations

smell: stateLockHint detects .terraform.tfstate.lock.info but only fires when tf init returns an error. Terraform's local backend places the lock during operations and removes it on success — a stale lock today usually means a prior crash. The hint message says 'run terraform force-unlock <id>' but provides NO way to extract the <id> automatically (it's in the lock.info JSON). Operators reading this hit the cookbook trail of 'how do I find the lock id', which they could read from the file directly.
fix_summary: Read the lock.info JSON, parse the .ID field, and substitute it into the message. Lock.info is small (~200 bytes) and fixed-shape (Terraform documents it). Net diff: +6 LOC, a sharper diagnostic.
rule_source: Go proverb: errors are values (the operator-actionable bit is the ID)
must_preserve: the symlink-aware lstat at the outer call sites; the no-auto-unlock policy

smell: StartWorkerVMs runs `tf apply -var start_workers_immediately=true -target=module.okd_cluster.proxmox_virtual_environment_vm.worker` — passing the override as a -var flag, NOT as a terraform.tfvars edit. The on-disk tfvars still says `start_workers_immediately = false` (or whatever the default was). The next `okdctl destroy --target=…worker[N]` re-applies tfvars cleanly, but a manual `terraform plan` from the workdir would diff against the in-memory -var override. Operators reading state-as-source-of-truth see a stale on-disk tfvars vs the actual cluster.
fix_summary: Either (a) regenerate tfvars with start_workers_immediately=true before the apply (matches setup.GenerateTerraformVars convention), or (b) document in the StartWorkerVMs doc that the on-disk tfvars is the deploy-time snapshot and runtime overrides flow through -var.

smell: Provider.Provision returns from terraform.Apply, then immediately calls retrieveProvisionResult which derives IPs by arithmetic — no readiness probe against Proxmox to confirm the VM is created and visible via the Proxmox API. The VMs may exist in tfstate before they're listable via `pvesh get /nodes/<n>/qemu`. Downstream callers (install.WaitForBootstrap) poll the IP — they will retry — but the immediate logger.Info('vm provisioned', ip) is misleading if the VM isn't yet enumerable.
evidence:
applyErr := p.terraformExec.Apply(ctx, applyOpts)
stopSpinner()
// ... no eventual-consistency probe before:
result, err := p.retrieveProvisionResult(cfg)
fix_summary: After Apply succeeds, run a single bounded `pvesh get /nodes/<node>/qemu` lookup to confirm vmid_base is enumerated. On miss, log Info 'vm not yet enumerable, install phase will retry' instead of the misleading 'provisioned' log. Mutation invariant remains intact (this is a read-only probe through pvesh, which is already used by phase.iso_cleanup.go).
rule_source: proxmox.go:23-29 (Mutation invariant — reads OK through pvesh)

smell: resolveProjectRootOrDie refuses any directory whose Base(cfgFile) is missing — defense-in-depth against running cleanup against the wrong root. But after a partial-failed deploy that wipes okdctl.yaml (cleanup.WorkDirectory removes the cluster-config dir first in Full kind), the operator can no longer run `okdctl destroy` because the marker is gone. The cluster's terraform state still exists, the VMs still exist, but okdctl refuses to recognise its own project. Recovery requires recreating an okdctl.yaml shell.
severity_reason: Recovery friction in a narrow case (yaml lost but state alive). The defense-in-depth use case (wrong-dir guard) is genuinely valuable; tightening it shouldn't weaken the security posture.
fix_summary: Accept any of {okdctl.yaml, okdctl.env, infrastructure/terraform/environments/<env>/terraform.tfstate} as a project marker — at least one is present after deploy starts. Document the broadened marker set in the doc comment so the security argument is preserved (any of these files only exists in an okdctl project).
rule_source: CLAUDE.md §security-invariants (allowlist-style critical path checks — the marker is one)

smell: runUpdateIngressDryRun prints the would-do list and returns nil. It does NOT consult the existing dnsmasq state. If on-disk dnsmasq config is currently in production-DNS mode (post-cutover) and an operator runs `okdctl update-ingress --dry-run` again, the dry-run preview says 'would deploy production dnsmasq config' even though it would be a no-op. Pure UX/recoverability gap — the dry-run lies about what the live run would do.
fix_summary: Have runUpdateIngressDryRun call dns.IsBootstrapDNS(cfg) and conditionally emit '(no-op: dns already cut over)' for the deploy-production-dnsmasq line. Same for haproxy: probe `system.IsServiceActive(ctx, haproxy)` and label that line accordingly.
rule_source: repo-counter-example: postinstall/update_ingress.go:70 (dns.IsBootstrapDNS used in live path)

smell: destroyTracker buffers failure labels for a final summary step but the tracker comment notes 'safe without a mutex because Orchestrator.Run iterates steps serially'. If a future patch parallelizes destroy (or an addon-cleanup phase adopts the tracker pattern) the failures slice corrupts. The comment hedges with 'add sync.Mutex if step parallelism ever lands' — a bare TODO without owner/issue per CLAUDE.md §code-comments.
fix_summary: Either (a) add a sync.Mutex now (3 LOC) and stop reasoning about parallelism, or (b) replace the comment with `// TODO(@qxtaiba): see #<issue>` linking a real issue per CLAUDE.md §code-comments.
